column1: What stud dimension range typically defines microscale Lego construction?
column2: Approximately 8 to 30 studs in any primary dimension for a complete assembly.

column1: At what scale ratios does microscale Lego construction typically operate?
What is the fundamental cognitive shift required to build effectively at microscale?
column2: The builder must see through individual parts to the aggregate volumetric impression they create, rather than mapping parts one-to-one to real objects.

column1: What is the core invariant governing all microscale work regarding proportion?
column2: Preservation of recognizable proportion despite radical reduction in geometric fidelity—communicating architectural identity through massing and silhouette rather than literal detail replication.

column1: How does real-world dimension per stud change between 1:200 and 1:500 scale?
column2: At 1:200, one stud ≈ 1.6 meters of real space; at 1:500, one stud ≈ 4 meters, since the stud is 8mm on center (7.8mm pitch).

column1: At 1:500 scale, how must a standard 2-meter doorway be represented, and why?
column2: Through color contrast or negative space rather than literal void geometry, because the doorway compresses to only two-fifths of a stud width—sub-stud scale and unrepresentable as physical geometry.

column1: What three hierarchical visual cues does the human visual system rely on for recognition at distance/reduced scale?
column2: Overall silhouette geometry, proportional relationships between major volumes, and high-contrast boundaries between forms.

column1: In microscale building, how does the priority of surface detail vs. compositional density invert compared to minifigure-scale building?
column2: Minifigure-scale prioritizes surface detail, texture, and ornament; microscale demands compositional density—strategic layering of primitives for volumetric mass and silhouette recognition before any surface detail.

column1: What is the core dimensional invariant (the 5:2 relationship) in LEGO plate-to-stud geometry?
column2: Five standard plates equal precisely two LEGO studs in height.

column1: What is 'dimensional anisotropy' in the context of LEGO microscale building?
column2: The directional dependence of resolution—horizontal resolution (measured in studs) operates at a fundamentally different granularity than vertical resolution (measured in plates), unlike a uniform digital pixel grid.

column1: How are smooth curves and diagonal slopes represented in LEGO microscale geometry?
column2: Through discrete stepping functions, since LEGO's quantized geometry cannot natively produce smooth curves; offsets are approximated via half-plate adjustments, jumper plates, or bracket elements.

column1: What question distinguishes a builder with internalized 'silhouette thinking' from a less advanced microscale builder?
column2: Instead of asking 'how can I represent this window?', they ask 'does this volume read correctly as the intended shape?'—prioritizing overall form recognition over literal feature replication.
